issues.legal_issue: The High Court may exercise supervisory jurisdiction over a tribunal order when it addresses legal questions affecting the tribunal’s authority without re-deciding accepted findings of fact.
material_facts: The tenant challenged the revenue tribunals’ orders in a proceeding under Article 227.

The High Court accepted the tribunals’ material factual findings and differed on the legal effect of the lease and the maintainability of the landlord’s application, matters affecting the tribunals’ authority to grant relief.
issues.conclusion: The High Court did not exceed its jurisdiction under Article 227.
issues.legal_principle: The supervisory powers under Article 227 are not greater than those under Article 226 and do not permit the High Court to sit in appeal over a tribunal; they are directed to ensuring that tribunals act within their authority. The Court applied Nagendra Nath Bora v. Commissioner of Hills Division and Appeals and Rambhau v. Shankar Singh.

predicates.supervisory_review_of_tribunal_order: A party sought supervisory review of an order made by a tribunal.
predicates.high_court_accepted_material_facts: The High Court accepted the tribunal’s material factual findings.
predicates.disagreement_concerned_tribunal_authorit: The High Court’s disagreement concerned legal matters affecting the tribunal’s authority to grant relief.

issues.definition: When supervisory review concerns a tribunal order, the High Court accepts the material facts, and its disagreement concerns the tribunal’s authority, its interference is within supervisory jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A mother may be treated as the natural guardian of her minor child in particular circumstances where the father, although alive, does not take an interest in the child’s affairs and the mother provides care and manages the child’s property.
material_facts: The child’s parents had separated and the father was not taking an interest in the child’s affairs.
The child lived under the mother’s care and protection, and the mother managed the child’s property by leasing it in the usual course.
The lease transaction was not shown to be imprudent or contrary to the child’s interests.
issues.conclusion: In the circumstances, the mother could be treated as the minor’s natural guardian, and the lease she granted on the minor’s behalf was valid and binding.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act, 1956 provides that the father is the natural guardian of a Hindu minor and, after him, the mother; the Court stated that the position under Hindu law before that Act was the same. On the facts, the mother was properly treated as the natural guardian, and there was no evidence that the lease was imprudent or not in the minor’s interest.

rule.if: minor_property_management_dispute and father_alive_but_disengaged and mother_cares_for_minor_and_manages_property and transaction_not_shown_adverse_to_minor

predicates.minor_property_management_dispute: A dispute concerns a transaction involving property belonging to a minor.
predicates.father_alive_but_disengaged: The father is alive but does not take an interest in the minor’s affairs.
predicates.mother_cares_for_minor_and_manages_prope: The mother cares for and protects the minor and manages the minor’s property.
predicates.transaction_not_shown_adverse_to_minor: The transaction is not shown to be imprudent or contrary to the minor’s interests.

issues.definition: In a dispute over a minor’s property, when the father is alive but disengaged, the mother cares for the minor and manages the property, and the transaction is not shown to harm the minor’s interests, the mother may be treated as natural guardian for that transaction.

issues.legal_issue: The special recovery remedy for a tenancy created on or after the statutory cutoff does not apply when a valid tenancy was created before that cutoff.
material_facts: The tenant had occupied the land under leases granted by the mother from 1951 onwards.
A written lease for the 1956–57 year was executed in favour of the minor represented by her mother.
The mother was competent to act as the minor’s natural guardian in the circumstances, and the lease was valid and binding.
The landlord sought termination of the tenancy and recovery of possession under the special statutory remedy.
issues.conclusion: Because the valid tenancy had been created before the statutory cutoff, the special remedy under section 39 did not apply. The Court did not decide whether the application would have been time-barred if that section applied.
issues.legal_principle: Section 39 of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands (Vidarbha Region) Act, 1958 concerns tenancies created not earlier than April 1, 1957. A valid lease created before that date does not meet that requirement. The Court noted that the question of limitation under section 39 did not arise once the provision was found inapplicable; the possible deemed-tenancy issue under section 6 would matter only if the earlier lease were invalid.

predicates.landlord_tenancy_recovery_proceeding: A landlord seeks termination of a tenancy and recovery of possession through a special tenancy-law remedy.
predicates.valid_tenancy_created_before_cutoff: A valid tenancy was created before the legally relevant cutoff for that special remedy.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks recovery through a special tenancy-law remedy and the valid tenancy predates the remedy’s cutoff, that special remedy is unavailable.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s application seeking possession for personal cultivation may be considered under the alternative statutory resumption route, which limits the extent of land recoverable.
material_facts: The landlord applied to terminate the tenancy and recover the entire land for personal cultivation, and later sought half the land in the alternative.
The special remedy relied on by the landlord was unavailable because the tenancy predated the relevant cutoff.
The High Court treated the application as one under the alternative resumption route and directed a remand to determine the recoverable portion under the statutory formula.
The landlord’s family holding and the area leased were considered in applying that formula.
issues.conclusion: The High Court correctly treated the application as one under sections 36 and 38 and remanded the matter to determine the portion recoverable under section 38; the landlord was not entitled to possession of the entire field under that route.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 38(4), proviso (i)(a), the landlord may resume for personal cultivation either one-third of the family holding or half of the land leased, whichever is greater. The Court held that the High Court’s directions to apply that formula on remand were correct.

rule.if: tenancy_resumption_application and landlord_seeks_personal_cultivation and special_recovery_route_unavailable and alternative_partial_resumption_route_available

predicates.tenancy_resumption_application: A landlord applies to terminate a tenancy and recover land from a tenant.
predicates.landlord_seeks_personal_cultivation: The landlord seeks the land for personal cultivation.
predicates.special_recovery_route_unavailable: The special recovery route invoked by the landlord is unavailable.
predicates.alternative_partial_resumption_route_ava: An alternative statutory route permits resumption of only a limited portion of the land.

issues.definition: When a landlord seeks land for personal cultivation in a tenancy resumption proceeding, the invoked special route is unavailable, and an alternative partial-resumption route is available, recovery is limited by the applicable formula.
